subject: Cognitive Science
title: Ad Hominem Attacks
description: A quick, practical guide to Ad Hominem Attacks.

hook.text: "Your argument about climate is wrong because you drive a big car." That attacks the person, not the point.

buildup.text: An ad hominem attacks the person making the argument instead of addressing the argument itself.

discovery.text: It's effective because we confuse the messenger with the message. A flawed person can make a valid point.

twist.text: Sometimes character is relevant—like questioning a witness's motive. But usually it's deflection, not logic.

climax.text: In politics, ad hominems dominate because they're emotionally powerful and logically empty.

punchline.text: Attack the argument, not the person.

quiz.question: What is an ad hominem fallacy?
options: Attacking the person instead of their argument
Agreeing with someone to avoid conflict

details.summary: An ad hominem attack targets the person making an argument rather than the argument itself. Dismissing a claim because the speaker is biased, inexperienced, or unlikable is a logical fallacy because the validity of an argument is independent of who presents it.
details.whyItMatters: Ad hominem attacks are the most common rhetorical fallacy. Recognizing them keeps you focused on the strength of arguments rather than the character of speakers.
takeaways: Attack the argument, not the person making it
A flawed messenger can still deliver a valid argument
Ad hominem is the most common fallacy in public discourse

faq.question: Is it ever relevant to question the source of an argument?
faq.answer: Yes, when the argument depends on the source's credibility, such as expert testimony. If a doctor recommends a treatment, their qualifications matter. But their argument's logic stands or falls independently.

faq.question: What are the main types of ad hominem?
faq.answer: Abusive attacks the person's character. Circumstantial points out that the person's situation makes them biased. Tu quoque accuses the person of hypocrisy. Guilt by association links the person to disliked groups. All redirect attention from the argument to the arguer.
